bom_multi_level.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all twelve sidecars change together.

engine.transform: float(); multiplied down the tree when collapsing; a falsy value becomes 1.0

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. Same rule as bom_single_level.consumption_rate, and more important here: multi-level rates multiply down the tree, so an estimate at level 3 propagates into every product above it.

columns.meaning: How much of this material the user buys from this supplier over one `time_unit`. A RATE, not a quantity — two rows are only comparable after both are converted to the same period.

engine.transform: rateToWeekly(volume, time_unit) — normalized to weeks

resolution.note: Volume is what the user's own systems recorded. It is not estimated; it is the thing other quantities are estimated FROM — demand_mean names it in estimable_from.

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `volume` is quoted over — day, week, month, quarter, year. It describes the VOLUME only. It says nothing about `lead_time`.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table

ingest.validate: one of day/week/month/quarter/year and their -ly spellings

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. Unrecognised or blank is read on a 7-day basis, i.e. as already weekly (grading.ts::rateToWeekly).

columns.name: lead_time
columns.meaning: How long this supplier takes to deliver this material. The contract fixes the unit at WEEKS; `time_unit` does not apply to it and never has.

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(lead_time, lead_time_unit), then round and clamp to [1, 51]

substitutions.when: the column is NULL or zero
substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: The engine already supports this split and has since scsim was written: SupplierLink carries lead_time_weeks (the CENTRE) separately from lead_time_dist and lead_time_cv (the SPREAD), and core/engine.py samples only when the distribution is not DETERMINISTIC and the CV is above zero. So deterministic is not a degenerate case bolted on — it is the default path, and it skips sampling entirely. default_mode is `asserted` for the same reason: the user states the lead time, and the spread is opt-in. estimable_from names the observations tier that does not exist yet (tier 2-O, reserved in WP 1.2) rather than leaving the door open to estimating this from whatever happens to be lying around.

columns.note: Was `unit_source: fixed` until WP 1.3, and fixed by OMISSION rather than by contract: the engine read a `lead_time_unit` that no column supplied, so every lead time was taken as weeks whatever the user meant. The column now exists and `unit` stays `weeks` because that is what NULL still means.

engine_requirement.reason: Supplier lead time per sourcing arc — missing values default to 2 weeks.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs from this supplier, delivered.

engine.transform: float(); a value <= 0 is replaced, not rejected

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

substitutions.value: this arc's price becomes the material's cost, via the cheapest inbound arc

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction.

columns.note: The user types `unit_price` and the engine calls it `cost`. Both names are recorded because the manual must lead with the one the user typed (D21).

engine_requirement.reason: Purchase cost per sourcing arc — a missing price defaults to 1.0 and distorts procurement spend.

columns.name: lead_time_unit

ingest.validate: one of the units public.unit_days() knows — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. NULL means weeks, matching project_map.py::_duration_to_weeks, and the column's CHECK constraint only admits units public.unit_days() knows.

columns.note: Added by WP 1.3 (D9). The engine had read this field since the scsim bridge was written; no column supplied it, so `r.get("lead_time_unit")` returned None on every row and a lead time entered in days was read as weeks — seven times too long, with no warning, because nothing in the chain knew a unit was expected. This is also the first use of the `contract` provenance state reserved in WP 1.2: the weeks default is supplied by this document, not guessed by code.

materials.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
materials.grain: One material in one project: the economics the simulation reads for it. The precision path — the CSV lanes carry prices too, and where this row is silent the engine derives the value from them rather than treating it as missing.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

columns.name: cost
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs to buy. The master value; where it is unset the engine uses the cheapest inbound arc instead, which is usually what the user wants and is why leaving it blank is not an error.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: the cheapest inbound unit_price for this material, floored at 1.0

substitutions.value: the cheapest inbound arc's unit_price (grading.ts::cheapestInboundCost floors a <= 0 price to 1.0 first)

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. estimable_from is empty for a second reason: the value already has a derivation — the cheapest inbound arc — and that is a substitution the user can see and trace, not an estimate.

engine_requirement.reason: Inventory valuation and holding cost — the terminal default of 1.0 makes every cost KPI meaningless.
engine_requirement.fallback: cheapest inbound unit_price across the material's suppliers

columns.name: holding_cost_pct
columns.unit: fraction of unit value per year
columns.meaning: The annual cost of holding one unit in stock, as a fraction of its value. 0.2 means holding a unit for a year costs a fifth of what the unit is worth.

engine.transform: falls back to the inventory policy bundle's holding_cost_pct when NULL
engine.missing_default: the project's inventory policy bundle value (0.2 in the shipped default)

resolution.note: A financial policy parameter, not an observation: it is what the business decides holding stock costs it. Falls back to the project's inventory bundle, which is a policy default and is visible as one.

columns.name: moq
columns.meaning: Minimum order quantity: the smallest amount this material can be ordered in. A commercial fact the supplier states, not something to be inferred from order history.

engine.transform: float(moq) when truthy, else 0.0 — applied per (supplier, material) link

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. A minimum order quantity is a term the supplier states. Inferring it from observed order sizes learns the ordering policy, not the constraint — and then the simulation optimises against its own past behaviour.

columns.name: initial_on_hand
columns.meaning: How much of this material is in stock when the simulation starts.

engine.transform: float() when not None; None is passed through as None, not as zero

resolution.note: Opening stock is a measurement — someone counted it — so it is the one master economic field where an observations tier could legitimately supply it. Nothing does today.

columns.name: lead_time_dist
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this material's delivery lead time — deterministic, or a named distribution around the arc's lead time. `deterministic` means the lead time is exactly what the arc says, every time.

engine.transform: LeadTimeDist(value) when set, else LeadTimeDist.DETERMINISTIC

ingest.validate: one of the LeadTimeDist enum values; `empirical` is reserved for the data-import path (M7) and is not selectable yet

resolution.note: The SPREAD half of lead_time's hybrid; the centre is inbound_logistics.lead_time. LeadTimeDist.EMPIRICAL exists in the enum and is RESERVED for the data-import path (M7) — it is the value an estimator would write, which is why it is not offered in the UI today. `deterministic` is the default and means the lead time is exactly what the arc says.

columns.name: lead_time_cv
columns.meaning: How much the lead time varies, as a coefficient of variation. Read only when `lead_time_dist` is not deterministic: the engine skips sampling entirely when the distribution is deterministic or the CV is zero.

engine.transform: float() when truthy, else 0.0

resolution.note: The magnitude of lead_time's spread. Read only when lead_time_dist is not deterministic: core/engine.py tests both, so a CV on a deterministic link is silently inert. Zero and NULL are the same thing here.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. columns.name: production_capacity
columns.meaning: How much of this product the plant can make per week. The canonical G4 example: when it is unset the engine invents a capacity generous enough that capacity never binds, so an unset value silently turns off the constraint the user thinks they are simulating.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: max(2 x demand, 1000) — a value chosen so the constraint never binds

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. This is the canonical G4 field: unset, the engine invents max(2 x demand, 1000), which is chosen so the constraint never binds. Estimating it from output would do the same thing with more ceremony — output is bounded by demand, so the fitted capacity can never explain a shortage.

engine_requirement.reason: With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds.

governance.note: `write: null` is literal: no page, edge function or upload path writes this table. It is loaded by an operator through the service role, which bypasses RLS — so the ABSENCE of an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE policy is the write rule, not an omission. Read is open to `authenticated` and `anon` because the risk shading renders on the public network pages.

A CHECK enforces the spelling so the unique index and the page lookup cannot disagree about whether 'Vietnam' and 'VIETNAM' are one country.

columns.name: risk_class
columns.meaning: The publisher's risk grade for the country, in the five-value vocabulary the map renders — Very Low, Low, Medium, High, Very High. An ordinal label, not a score: it may be compared for order and never averaged.

substitutions.when: no row exists for the node's country
substitutions.value: the map renders the node grey and labels it "Unknown"
substitutions.visible_as: RiskDataNotice — the page says the dimension is missing rather than shading it away

ingest.validate: one of Very Low / Low / Medium / High / Very High — CHECK risk_data_risk_class_known

columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and that is correct: country risk shades the network map, it is not a simulation input. `scsim` has no country concept — disruption targets are suppliers, plants and lanes (blueprint §2.3 G11). A later package that wants country risk to DRIVE anything must add it to the engine first, not read this column from the mapper. 'Unknown' is deliberately not a storable value: it is what the absence of a row looks like, and storing it would turn "we have no figure" into a figure (§5 T1; the same over-claim as D17).

columns.name: source
columns.meaning: Who published the figure — the named index or provider. NOT NULL because a country-risk grade with no named origin is an assertion the product cannot defend, and its only output is a colour a reader will take for fact.

columns.name: vintage
columns.meaning: The edition the figure is from, as the publisher labels it (e.g. "2025-H1"). This is the table's version axis: reference data is versioned by vintage, not by project (PLAN.md §2).

columns.name: licence
columns.meaning: The licence the row is held under. NOT NULL, and the reason is specific: country-risk indices are mostly commercial, so a row whose licence is unrecorded is a row nobody can tell you may republish — including in an export (§5 T4).

risk_data.note: The second of WP 1.4's three orphans (D4), and the one that turned out not to be an orphan at all. Two network pages read it and no migration created it — but the table EXISTS in the production database, untracked, with the spreadsheet-header columns `COUNTRY` and `"RISK CLASS"`. CI proved it: the first version of the migration was a plain `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which no-opped, and the next statement failed on a column that was not there. Same class as `approved_users`: created outside migration tracking, invisible to a static replay, which can only tell you no migration creates a table and not whether one exists. `20260915000003_risk_data.sql` now both builds it on a fresh database and ADOPTS the one already there — renaming the quoted columns, adding the provenance columns, and marking the pre-contract rows `source: 'unrecorded (loaded before the reference-tier contract)'` rather than inventing a publisher for them. The new CHECKs land `NOT VALID` on the adopted table: enforced for every future write, not retroactively asserted about rows nobody has looked at.

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning.

columns.name: from_location
columns.meaning: The upstream end of the edge — a supplier, a material, or the plant, depending on which lane produced it.

engine.consumed_by: network pages and the analyzers; not read by the engine mapping
engine.transform: copied from the lane row's id column

columns.name: to_location
columns.meaning: The downstream end of the edge.

engine.consumed_by: network pages and the analyzers; not read by the engine mapping
engine.transform: copied from the lane row's id column

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant this edge belongs to, by NAME — the join key G1 forbids. Renamed from `plant` by 20250822025432, which is also when its incorrect UNIQUE constraint stopped meaning one-row-per-plant.

engine.transform: copied from the lane row

columns.name: weighted
columns.meaning: The volume on this edge after unit normalization — always per WEEK, whatever period the uploaded row quoted. This is where D2's fix lands: before it, a supplier quoting 52 000 a year and one quoting 1 000 a week were summed as 52 000 and 1 000.

engine.consumed_by: the analyzers and the policy grid's volume basis; not the engine mapping
engine.transform: weeklyVolume(volume, time_unit) in _shared/laneVolumes.ts, over grading.ts's one unit table

columns.note: numeric(16,6) since 20250816031317. Normalization SHRINKS every value quoted coarser than a day and multiplies day-quoted rows by 7, so overflow needs a pre-existing value above ~1.43e9 in a day-quoted project. Bounded by analysis, not measurement — the §15 baseline has never been run.

columns.name: material_consumption_rate
columns.unit: units of upstream per unit of downstream
columns.meaning: How much of the upstream item one unit of the downstream item consumes, carried through from the BOM.

engine.consumed_by: the analyzers and the network pages; not the engine mapping
engine.transform: copied from bom consumption_rate, multiplied down multi-level chains

columns.name: sourcing_ratio
columns.unit: fraction of the destination's inbound flow
columns.meaning: This edge's share of everything flowing into its destination. A share, so the D2 unit error did not cancel: it decides which supplier the platform calls primary.

engine.consumed_by: the policy grid's primary-source suggestion; the analyzers
engine.transform: volumeShare(weeklyVolume(row), weeklyVolumeTotalsBy(...)) in _shared/laneVolumes.ts

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the edge was first computed. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the edge was last recomputed. Server-set.

columns.name: is_critical_node
columns.meaning: Whether an analyzer flagged this edge's node as critical. An analysis result stored on an entity row — exactly the smearing D19 names.
columns.note: NOT an engine input. It is analyzer output written onto a tier-3 entity row with no identity, no version and no input hash (D19). WP 4.2 moves it to `analysis_results`; WP 5.3 drops the column. Recorded here so the move has a starting inventory.

columns.name: critical_node_score
columns.meaning: The score behind `is_critical_node`.
columns.note: Analyzer output smeared onto the entity row (D19). See is_critical_node.

columns.name: prediction_timestamp
columns.meaning: When the criticality prediction was made. The closest thing this table has to a version stamp, and it names no model and no input hash.
columns.note: Analyzer output smeared onto the entity row (D19). See is_critical_node.

columns.name: uploaded_by
columns.meaning: The user whose upload produced this edge. Referenced by the RLS policies.
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. Read by this table's RLS policies, which grant on `uploaded_by = get_current_user_id() AND organization = get_current_user_org()`.

columns.name: organization
columns.meaning: The owning organization, as a NAME with a `default_org` default. A displayable string used as an authorization key — the second half of G1, and the identity D13 says is compared by string.
columns.note: Governance, not a parameter. WP 2.1 replaces it with an org uuid.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this edge belongs to. NULLABLE here, unlike every lane table — a row with no project is reachable only through the organization/uploader policies.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

columns.name: data_source
columns.meaning: Which lane produced this edge — inbound, outbound or BOM.

engine.consumed_by: the network pages, to colour and filter edges by origin
engine.transform: set by the ETL per lane

columns.name: data_source_group
columns.meaning: A coarser grouping of `data_source`, for filtering.

engine.transform: set by the ETL per lane

columns.name: is_zero_flow_filtered
columns.meaning: Whether this edge was hidden for carrying no flow in either direction.

engine.consumed_by: the network pages, to exclude dead edges from the drawn graph
engine.transform: set by the ETL

columns.name: zero_flow_filter_applied_at
columns.meaning: When the zero-flow filter last ran over this edge.
columns.note: ETL bookkeeping; not an engine input and not analyzer output.

columns.name: zero_flow_filter_reason
columns.meaning: Why the edge was filtered. One value is used today: zero_incoming_outgoing_flow.
columns.note: ETL bookkeeping; not an engine input and not analyzer output.

supply_chain_data_multi_tier.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
supply_chain_data_multi_tier.grain: One edge of the DEEP supply graph — tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers behind the direct ones. Computed by the same ETL, read by the network pages, and NOT propagated into the simulation: the engine models a single focal plant with three echelons (blueprint §2.4).

governance.note: Written by the `combine-project` edge function, never by a page. Invariant I2: pages never write tier 3. `write: null` is therefore a statement, not an omission — there is no user-facing write path and there must not be one.

columns.name: level
columns.meaning: How many tiers upstream of the plant this edge sits. 2 is a supplier's supplier.

engine.transform: int()

columns.meaning: The direct (tier-1) supplier this deep chain hangs off, so a deep edge can be attributed to a supplier the plant actually buys from.

engine.transform: set by the ETL while walking the chain
